transcript.text: my tumble dryer is giving off a burning smell?? is it safe to keep using it

No, stop using it for now. A burning smell from a tumble dryer is a fire risk, and dryer fires are common. Until you know the cause, treat it as unsafe.

## What to do right now
1. Turn it off and unplug it at the wall (or switch off the isolator if it's hardwired).
2. Take the clothes out and check they're not hot or scorched.
3. If you see smoke, sparks, or flames, get out and call the fire brigade (999 in the UK). Don't open the door if there's a fire inside, as that feeds it oxygen.
4. Let it cool fully before inspecting anything.

## Common causes (roughly most to least likely)
• Lint buildup. This is the big one. Fluff collects in the filter, the filter housing, and behind/under the drum near the heating element, where it can scorch or ignite.
• Blocked or kinked vent hose (vented dryers). Hot air can't escape, so the machine overheats.
• Full water tank or clogged condenser (condenser dryers), which also causes overheating.
• Worn drive belt. Often a rubbery burning smell, sometimes with squealing or the drum not turning.
• Failing motor or heating element, or a faulty thermostat/thermal fuse.
• Something caught in the drum (a sock, tissue, or a lighter left in a pocket).
• Burnt-on residue from fabric softener sheets or something greasy/oily in the load. Note that items with oil residue (cooking oil, massage oil, petrol) can actually self-ignite in a dryer.
• A brand-new dryer can smell for the first few uses as factory coatings burn off. This is normal if it fades quickly.

## Safe checks you can do yourself (unplugged)
• Clean the lint filter thoroughly, and vacuum out the slot it sits in.
• Check the vent hose isn't crushed, kinked, or full of fluff, and that the outside vent flap opens freely.
• For condenser dryers: empty the water tank and rinse the condenser unit under the tap.
• Look inside the drum and around the door seal for anything stuck.
• Sniff around the back/bottom for where the smell is strongest.

## Call an engineer if
• The smell continues after cleaning
• It smells electrical (sharp, plasticky, "hot wires")
• You hear squealing, grinding, or the drum isn't turning
• It's tripping your electrics
• There's any visible scorching

## Also worth checking
Look up your model for a safety recall. There have been major ones in the UK (for example, Whirlpool's Hotpoint, Indesit, Creda, Swan and Proline models, where lint could contact the heating element). You can check on the manufacturer's website or the UK government's Product Safety Database.

Both of those are bad, but it's actually good news, because together they very likely explain the smell. A singed dust/hair smell is the classic sign of lint getting too hot.

## Why it's a problem
• Full lint filter: air can't flow, so the dryer runs hotter and fluff gets pushed into the machine, where it can collect near the heating element and scorch.
• Squashed hose: hot, damp, lint-filled air can't escape, so heat and fluff build up inside. This is a common cause of dryer fires.

## How to fix it (keep it unplugged)
1. Clean the filter properly. Pull off all the fluff, and if it looks clogged or waxy (from fabric softener), wash it in warm soapy water and let it dry fully.
2. Vacuum the filter slot with a crevice tool. Fluff often builds up deep in there.
3. Sort out the hose:
• Disconnect it and check inside for lint. Shake or vacuum it out.
• If it's crushed, split, or won't hold its shape, replace it. They're cheap (usually about £10–15 for a standard 4"/100mm hose).
• When you put it back, keep it as short and straight as possible, with no kinks, and don't push the dryer flat against the wall.
4. Check the outside vent (if it goes through a wall or window). Make sure the flap opens freely and isn't blocked with fluff.

## Testing it afterwards
• Run a short, empty or light load while you stay nearby.
• If there's no burning smell, you've likely fixed it. Clean the filter after every load from now on.
• If the smell comes back, stop using it. Lint has probably built up inside the machine near the heating element, which needs an engineer (or replacement, given it's 7 years old).

It's also worth putting your model number into the Electrical Safety First product recall checker or Beko's website, just to rule out any safety notices.
